passage:
Subject: Terms we agreed by phone

Dear Jatin,

Thank you for the draft of the design contract. I've compared it with our call on Tuesday and I noticed three differences. The scope you described on the phone included two rounds of revisions, but the draft doesn't say how many. The "handling charge" in the last paragraph was never mentioned. And you said the second payment would come within a week of delivery, but the draft says "at our convenience."

Before I sign, please put all three in writing as we agreed on the call. I'm keeping our messages as a record.

I also understand you'd like me to sign today. I'd rather take the time to be sure. If the terms can't be written down, I'll have to decline.

Sincerely,
Amandeep

qa.q: How many differences did Amandeep find between the call and the draft?
qa.a: Amandeep found three differences: the revisions, the handling charge and the payment timing.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep refuse to sign the same day?
qa.a: Amandeep felt uneasy that spoken promises were missing from the paper and pressure to sign today is a red flag, so Amandeep wanted time to check.

qa.q: What small steps helped Amandeep protect against deceit?
qa.a: Amandeep listed the differences, asked for them in writing, kept messages as a record and said clearly that unwritten terms mean a no.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the email?
qa.a: Jatin may feel caught out or irritated, but an honest party would see the request as fair, since it only asks that the phone terms be put on paper.

grounding: Amandeep notices hidden fees, vague scope and verbal promises missing on paper, insists on written terms, keeps records and resists pressure to sign today.
